name: AI Foundations with ChatGPT
level: Business course · no official exam yet
audience: Professionals in any role who use ChatGPT for everyday work: drafting, summarising, analysis, research and simple automation. No coding needed.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test. OpenAI's own certification is in invite-only pilot; this course follows the topics of OpenAI Academy's free courses.

domains.name: How LLMs work and their limits
domains.summary: What a large language model is, how it produces text, and the limits that follow: hallucination, knowledge cutoffs, context windows and non-determinism.

domains.name: Prompting for work
domains.summary: Writing prompts that get usable results the first time: goal, context, audience, format, examples and constraints, then iterating.

domains.name: Checking and improving output
domains.summary: Verifying facts, numbers and sources; spotting bias and gaps; asking ChatGPT to critique and revise; deciding when output is good enough to use.

domains.name: ChatGPT features and workflows
domains.summary: Picking the right ChatGPT tool for the job: projects, memory, custom GPTs, apps (connectors), file and data analysis, canvas, search, deep research, image and voice.

domains.name: Agents and automation basics
domains.summary: What agents are, when to delegate multi-step work to agent mode or deep research, and where human checkpoints belong.

domains.name: Safe and responsible use
domains.summary: Data sensitivity, workspace admin and data controls, company policy, disclosure, bias, intellectual property and staying accountable for what you ship.

scenarios.title: Marketing manager
scenarios.description: Drafts campaign copy, summarises customer research and builds briefs. Needs on-brand output and must avoid publishing unverified claims.

scenarios.title: Finance analyst
scenarios.description: Uploads spreadsheets for analysis and charts. Must check every number and keep confidential figures inside approved tools.

scenarios.title: HR business partner
scenarios.description: Rewrites policies, prepares interview guides and answers employee questions. Handles personal data and must watch for bias.

scenarios.title: Sales operations lead
scenarios.description: Preps account research, call notes and follow-up emails, and is exploring agents to automate repetitive research.

scenarios.title: Team lead rolling out ChatGPT
scenarios.description: Sets up shared projects and custom GPTs for a team and writes the team’s do and don’t guidelines.

lessons.title: What an LLM actually does
lessons.summary: A large language model predicts likely next words from patterns in its training data. That single fact explains most of its strengths and failures.

sections.heading: Prediction, not lookup
sections.body:
A large language model (LLM) such as the GPT models behind ChatGPT is trained on huge amounts of text to predict what text should come next. It doesn't look facts up in a database by default; it generates text that **fits the patterns** it learned.

That's why it is excellent at drafting, rephrasing, summarising and explaining, and why it can produce fluent text that is wrong.

sections.heading: Tokens and the context window
sections.body:
Models read and write in **tokens** (chunks of words). Everything the model can "see" in a conversation (your messages, uploaded files, its own replies, instructions) has to fit in its **context window**.

- Very long chats or huge files can push early details out of view or dilute attention.
- When a long conversation starts drifting, start a fresh chat with a short summary of what matters.

sections.heading: Knowledge cutoff and tools
sections.body:
A model's built-in knowledge stops at its **training cutoff**. For anything recent (prices, news, policies, product versions) use ChatGPT's **search** or **deep research**, or give it the source document yourself.

When ChatGPT uses search, it shows sources. Open them: a citation shows where a claim came from, not that the claim is right.

sections.heading: Same prompt, different answers
sections.body: Generation involves sampling, so the same prompt can give different wording or even different conclusions. Treat the first answer as a draft. For decisions, ask for reasoning, alternatives and sources, and compare.

keyPoints: LLMs generate likely text; they are not databases of facts.
Everything in the chat must fit in the context window; long chats degrade.
Built-in knowledge has a cutoff; use search, deep research or your own documents for current facts.
Outputs vary between runs: treat answers as drafts.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a confident, well-written answer is accurate.
gotchas.correct: Fluency is not accuracy. Verify facts, figures and quotes, especially ones you will publish or act on.

gotchas.trap: Asking about last month’s news without turning on search.
gotchas.correct: Use search or deep research, or paste the source, for anything after the model’s cutoff.

lessons.lab: Ask ChatGPT the same question three times in three new chats: "What are the three biggest risks for a mid-size retailer adopting AI?" Compare the answers. Which points repeat? Which appear only once? Write one sentence on what that tells you about trusting a single answer.

lessons.title: Hallucinations and other failure modes
lessons.summary: Know the ways ChatGPT goes wrong so you can catch them before they reach a customer or a decision.

sections.heading: Hallucination
sections.body:
A **hallucination** is confident, plausible content that is false: an invented statistic, a quote nobody said, a court case that doesn't exist, a wrong product feature.

Risk is highest for **specific details**: names, numbers, dates, citations, legal or medical specifics, and niche topics with little training data.

sections.heading: Other common failures
sections.body:
- **Sycophancy:** agreeing with you because you sounded sure. Ask it to argue the other side.
- **Over-generalising:** turning one example into a rule.
- **Missing context:** it can't know your company's policies, numbers or customers unless you provide them.
- **Arithmetic and counting slips** in plain text: ask it to use data analysis (it runs code) for calculations.
- **Bias** inherited from training data, in wording, examples or assumptions about people.

sections.heading: Reducing the risk
sections.body:
- Give it the source material and tell it to answer **only from the provided documents**, saying "not in the source" when something is missing.
- Ask for **quotes or page references** for key claims.
- For numbers, upload the data and have it compute with data analysis rather than estimate.
- Allow uncertainty: "If you are not sure, say so."

keyPoints: Hallucinations cluster in specifics: numbers, names, dates, citations.
Grounding answers in provided documents and asking for quotes reduces risk.
Use data analysis (code) for calculations, not mental arithmetic.
Invite disagreement to counter sycophancy.

gotchas.trap: Asking ChatGPT "Are you sure?" and accepting "Yes" as verification.
gotchas.correct: Self-confirmation is not verification. Check the claim against a primary source.

gotchas.trap: Letting it total a long column of numbers in plain chat.
gotchas.correct: Upload the file and ask it to calculate with data analysis, then spot-check the result.

lessons.lab: Paste a one-page document and ask: "Answer only from this document. Quote the sentence that supports each answer. If the document doesn't say, reply 'not in the source'." Then ask two questions the document does answer and one it doesn't. Did it hold the line on the third?

lessons.title: Anatomy of a good work prompt
lessons.summary: Most weak output comes from weak briefs. Brief ChatGPT like a smart new colleague who knows nothing about your situation.

sections.heading: The six parts
sections.body:
A strong prompt usually covers:

1. **Goal:** what you're trying to achieve and why.
2. **Context:** background, audience, constraints, what already exists.
3. **Role or perspective** (optional): "Act as a skeptical CFO reviewing this."
4. **Task:** the specific deliverable.
5. **Format:** length, structure, tone, headings, table, bullet count.
6. **Quality bar:** what good looks like, what to avoid.

sections.heading: Before and after
sections.body:
Weak:

```
Write an email about the new expense policy.
```

Strong:

```
You're writing to 40 field sales reps who submit expenses from their phones.
Goal: get them to use the new expense app from 1 March; old forms will be rejected.
Write a friendly email under 150 words with: a one-line summary, 3 bullet steps
to get started, the deadline in bold, and who to contact (finance-help@).
Avoid jargon and don't mention the old vendor.
```

sections.heading: Structure long prompts
sections.body:
For longer briefs, separate parts with headings or tags so instructions don't blur into source material:

```
## Instructions
Summarise the customer interviews below for the product team.
## Output
Top 5 themes, each with a supporting quote and how many interviews mentioned it.
## Interviews
[paste here]
```

sections.heading: Say what to do, not only what not to do
sections.body: "Write in short, plain sentences for a general audience" works better than a list of prohibitions. Positive instructions give the model a target.

keyPoints: Brief it like a capable new colleague: goal, context, task, format, quality bar.
Name the audience and the purpose.
Specify length and structure explicitly.
Separate instructions from pasted material with headings.
Positive instructions beat lists of don’ts.

gotchas.trap: One-line prompts for important deliverables.
gotchas.correct: Spend a minute on context and format. It saves several rounds of rework.

gotchas.trap: "Make it better."
gotchas.correct: Say what better means: shorter, more formal, for executives, with numbers, fewer bullets.

lessons.lab: Take a real task from this week. Write the prompt you'd normally use, run it, then rewrite it with all six parts and run that. Compare the two outputs and note how many edits each would need.

lessons.title: Examples, iteration and breaking work down
lessons.summary: Show what you want, iterate in small steps, and split big jobs into stages you can check.

sections.heading: Show, don’t only tell
sections.body: Paste one or two **examples** of the style or format you want ("Here are two past newsletters we liked"). Models imitate examples closely, so pick good ones and vary them if you don't want everything to look identical.

sections.heading: Iterate like an editor
sections.body:
Treat the first answer as a draft and give **specific feedback**:

- "Keep sections 1 and 3, rewrite 2 for a non-technical reader."
- "Cut to 120 words without losing the deadline."
- "Give me three alternative subject lines, more urgent."

If a chat goes off track after many turns, start a new chat with a clean, complete brief.

sections.heading: Decompose big tasks
sections.body:
For a large deliverable, go in stages and check each one:

1. Outline → you approve.
2. Draft each section → you review.
3. Tighten and format.

Stages catch wrong directions early and keep each request focused.

sections.heading: Ask it to ask you
sections.body: When you're not sure what context matters: "Before you start, ask me up to five questions you need answered to do this well."

keyPoints: One or two good examples shape style and format strongly.
Give targeted edit instructions, not vague dissatisfaction.
Split big work into outline, draft and polish stages.
Let ChatGPT interview you for missing context.
Restart with a clean brief when a long chat drifts.

gotchas.trap: Asking for a 20-page report in one prompt.
gotchas.correct: Outline first, then draft section by section, checking as you go.

gotchas.trap: Correcting the same mistake again and again in a long, messy chat.
gotchas.correct: Start a fresh chat with a complete brief that includes the correction.

lessons.lab: Ask ChatGPT to interview you ("ask me 5 questions first") before drafting a one-page project update. Then produce it in two stages: outline, then full draft. Note which of its questions surfaced context you would have left out.

lessons.title: Prompt patterns for everyday tasks
lessons.summary: Reusable patterns for summarising, drafting, analysing, brainstorming and preparing for meetings.

sections.heading: Summarise for a purpose
sections.body:
```
Summarise this 30-page vendor proposal for our COO, who has 2 minutes.
Give: price and term, the 3 biggest risks to us, anything that differs from
our RFP requirements, and a one-line recommendation. Quote clause numbers.
```

sections.heading: Draft in your voice
sections.body: Paste a few of your own past emails and say "Match this tone." Or save tone preferences in **custom instructions** or a **project** so every chat starts with them.

sections.heading: Analyse and decide
sections.body: Ask for **options with trade-offs**, not one answer: "Give three ways to reduce onboarding time, each with cost, effort, risk and what we'd need to believe for it to work."

sections.heading: Brainstorm widely, then narrow
sections.body: Ask for many ideas fast ("20 webinar titles"), then a second step to score them against your criteria. Separating generation from judgment gives better variety.

sections.heading: Meeting prep
sections.body: "Here are the agenda and last meeting's notes. List the decisions we need, likely objections from finance, and three questions I should ask."

keyPoints: Summaries should name the reader and what they need to decide.
Ask for options with trade-offs, not a single answer.
Generate broadly first, then evaluate in a separate step.
Store recurring tone and context in custom instructions or a project.

gotchas.trap: "Summarise this" with no audience or purpose.
gotchas.correct: Say who will read it, how long they have and what they need to decide.

lessons.lab: Build a personal prompt library: write one reusable prompt each for summarising, drafting an email, comparing options and meeting prep. Save them where you can reuse them (for example in a project's instructions or a notes doc).

lessons.title: Verifying facts, numbers and sources
lessons.summary: A practical routine for checking ChatGPT output before you use it, scaled to the stakes.

sections.heading: Scale checking to the stakes
sections.body:
- **Low stakes** (brainstorm, internal first draft): skim for sense.
- **Medium** (internal decisions, team docs): check key facts and numbers.
- **High** (customers, executives, legal, medical, financial, public): verify every claim against a **primary source** and have a qualified person review.

sections.heading: The checking routine
sections.body:
1. **Highlight checkable claims:** numbers, names, dates, quotes, "studies show".
2. **Open the sources** ChatGPT cites. Confirm the source exists, is credible and actually says that.
3. **Recompute numbers** from the data, or have data analysis show its working, then spot-check.
4. **Check against your own knowledge** and internal systems of record.
5. **Look for what's missing:** risks, counterarguments, affected groups.

sections.heading: Ask for evidence up front
sections.body: "For each claim, give the source and a direct quote." "Separate what the document says from your own inferences." These make checking faster and expose weak claims.

keyPoints: Match verification effort to how the output will be used.
Open cited sources and confirm they say what is claimed.
Recompute or spot-check every number that matters.
Ask for quotes and a split between facts and inferences.
High-stakes content needs a qualified human reviewer.

gotchas.trap: Treating a link in the answer as proof.
gotchas.correct: Open it. Sources can be misread, outdated, low quality or not say what the answer claims.

gotchas.trap: Sending AI-written numbers to a client unchecked.
gotchas.correct: Recompute from the source data before anything leaves the team.

lessons.lab: Ask ChatGPT with search for "5 statistics about remote work productivity with sources". Check each one: does the source exist, is it credible, does it say exactly that, and how old is it? Score how many survive.

lessons.title: Critiquing and improving drafts
lessons.summary: Use ChatGPT as an editor and reviewer, with clear criteria, while keeping your own judgment in charge.

sections.heading: Review against criteria
sections.body: Give explicit criteria: "Review this proposal as a skeptical procurement lead. Score clarity, evidence, risks addressed and call to action from 1–5, explain each score, then list the three changes that would raise the scores most."

sections.heading: Fresh eyes beat self-review
sections.body: A model asked to review what it just wrote in the same chat tends to defend it. For an honest critique, paste the draft into a **new chat** (or ask a colleague) with the review criteria.

sections.heading: Check for bias and gaps
sections.body: Ask: "Who might be left out or treated unfairly by this text? What assumptions does it make about the reader?" Review job ads, policies and customer messages for exclusionary wording.

sections.heading: Know when to stop
sections.body: Endless polishing has diminishing returns. Decide upfront what "good enough" means for this use, check it against that, and ship.

keyPoints: Critiques are better with explicit criteria and a reviewer persona.
Review in a fresh chat to avoid the model defending its own draft.
Ask directly about bias, exclusion and hidden assumptions.
Define "good enough" before you start polishing.

gotchas.trap: Asking the same chat that wrote the draft to grade it.
gotchas.correct: Use a fresh chat or another reviewer with clear criteria.

lessons.lab: Write (or have ChatGPT write) a short job ad. In a new chat, ask for a review for clarity, inclusive language and unnecessary requirements. Apply the changes you agree with and note any you rejected and why.

lessons.title: Choosing the right ChatGPT tool
lessons.summary: ChatGPT is a set of tools. Picking the right one for the task matters as much as the prompt.

sections.heading: The toolkit (names and plan availability change: check the current help center)
sections.body:
- **Chat:** quick questions, drafting, rewriting.
- **Search:** current information with cited sources.
- **Deep research:** a multi-step research agent that reads many sources and returns a cited report; takes minutes, not seconds.
- **File uploads and data analysis:** read documents; analyse spreadsheets by running code; produce charts and files.
- **Canvas:** a side-by-side editor for longer writing and code you want to edit together.
- **Image generation and editing:** visuals, mock-ups, diagrams.
- **Voice:** talk through ideas hands-free.
- **Agent mode:** ChatGPT uses its own browser and tools to carry out multi-step tasks, asking before consequential actions.

sections.heading: Match the task
sections.body:
| Task | Best fit |
|---|---|
| Draft a reply | Chat |
| What changed in a regulation this year | Search or deep research |
| Analyse 6 months of sales data | Data analysis with the uploaded file |
| Co-write a long proposal | Canvas |
| Compare 15 vendors' public pricing pages | Deep research or agent mode |

sections.heading: Models and reasoning
sections.body: ChatGPT offers faster models and slower **reasoning** ("thinking") modes. Use fast for everyday drafting; use reasoning for complex analysis, planning, maths and tricky trade-offs. Exact model names change often, so learn the trade-off rather than the names.

keyPoints: Search and deep research are for current or sourced information.
Data analysis runs code on your files: use it for calculations and charts.
Canvas is for longer documents you edit with ChatGPT.
Reasoning modes trade speed for better multi-step thinking.
Agent mode carries out multi-step tasks and asks before consequential actions.

gotchas.trap: Using plain chat to answer questions about this week’s events.
gotchas.correct: Turn on search or use deep research for current information.

gotchas.trap: Using deep research for a quick factual lookup.
gotchas.correct: Deep research takes minutes; use search for quick lookups.

lessons.lab: Do one small task with each of: search, data analysis (upload a CSV), canvas and image generation. For each, write one line on when you'd use it again.

lessons.title: Projects, memory, custom GPTs and apps
lessons.summary: Stop re-explaining context: organise recurring work with projects, memory, custom instructions, custom GPTs and connected apps.

sections.heading: Custom instructions and memory
sections.body: **Custom instructions** tell ChatGPT about you and how you like answers (role, tone, format) for every chat. **Memory** lets ChatGPT remember useful details across chats; you can view, edit, delete or turn it off, and use a temporary chat when you don't want history or memory used.

sections.heading: Projects
sections.body: A **project** groups related chats, files and instructions in one place: a client, a product launch, a recurring report. Files and instructions in the project apply to every chat in it, and projects can be shared with teammates on workspace plans. Projects can keep memory scoped to the project so context doesn't leak between unrelated work.

sections.heading: Custom GPTs
sections.body: A **GPT** is a reusable, configured version of ChatGPT with its own instructions, knowledge files and capabilities, for a repeated job: "Brand voice editor", "RFP first-draft writer". Share it with your team so everyone gets consistent results. Keep instructions specific and knowledge files current.

sections.heading: Apps (formerly connectors)
sections.body: **Apps** connect ChatGPT to tools such as email, calendars, drives and work systems so it can search and use your data in answers, deep research or agent tasks. Access follows your permissions in those tools, and workspace admins control which apps are allowed.

sections.heading: Choosing between them
sections.body:
- Preference that applies everywhere → custom instructions.
- Ongoing piece of work with files → project.
- Repeatable task others should run the same way → custom GPT.
- Needs live company data → app connection (if your admin allows it).

keyPoints: Custom instructions apply to every chat; memory is viewable and controllable.
Projects bundle chats, files and instructions for ongoing work.
Custom GPTs package a repeatable task for consistent team use.
Apps connect ChatGPT to your tools, respecting your permissions and admin settings.
Use temporary chats when you don’t want history or memory involved.

gotchas.trap: Pasting the same background into every new chat.
gotchas.correct: Put it in a project’s instructions and files, or in custom instructions.

gotchas.trap: Building a custom GPT for a one-off task.
gotchas.correct: GPTs pay off for repeated, shared tasks. One-offs belong in a normal chat or project.

lessons.lab: Create a project for one recurring piece of work. Add two reference files and instructions (audience, tone, format). Run two different requests in it and check that both follow the instructions without you repeating them.

lessons.title: Agents: delegating multi-step work
lessons.summary: Agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks with tools. Delegate well-defined work, and keep humans at the checkpoints that matter.

sections.heading: What an agent is
sections.body: An **agent** is an AI system that works toward a goal over several steps, deciding what to do next and using **tools** (browsing, files, apps, code) along the way. In ChatGPT, **deep research** (research tasks) and **agent mode** (research plus actions in a browser and connected apps) are agent-style features.

sections.heading: Good tasks to delegate
sections.body:
- Clear goal and finish line: "Compile a table of the 10 largest competitors' public pricing, with links."
- Tolerant of a draft-quality result you'll review.
- Low risk if a step goes wrong, or with a confirmation before anything consequential.

Poor fits: vague goals, high-stakes irreversible actions without review, tasks needing judgment the agent can't access.

sections.heading: Human checkpoints
sections.body: Design where a person approves: before purchases, before sending messages to customers, before changing records, before publishing. ChatGPT's agent asks for confirmation before consequential actions; you can also watch it and take over. **You remain accountable** for what it does on your behalf.

sections.heading: From prompts to workflows
sections.body: Think in workflows: input → steps → checkpoint → output. Start with a single prompt, turn a repeated one into a project or custom GPT, then consider agents or scheduled tasks for multi-step routines. Measure time saved and error rate before scaling.

keyPoints: Agents pursue a goal over many steps using tools.
Delegate tasks with a clear goal, finish line and tolerable risk.
Put human approval before consequential or irreversible actions.
You stay accountable for what an agent does for you.
Grow from prompt → reusable prompt or GPT → agent workflow.

gotchas.trap: Letting an agent send customer emails or make purchases with no review.
gotchas.correct: Require confirmation before consequential actions and review results.

gotchas.trap: Giving an agent a vague goal like "improve our marketing".
gotchas.correct: Define the deliverable, sources, constraints and what done looks like.

lessons.lab: Write an agent brief for a research task: goal, sources to use or avoid, output format, and when to stop and ask you. Run it with deep research or agent mode and list which parts of the brief it followed and which it missed.

lessons.title: Data, privacy and workspace controls
lessons.summary: Know what you can share, which ChatGPT plan your company approved, and the controls that protect data.

sections.heading: Follow your company policy first
sections.body: Use the ChatGPT workspace your organisation approved (for example a Business, Enterprise or Edu workspace) for work data, not a personal account. Your company's data classification rules decide what can go in. When in doubt, leave it out or ask.

sections.heading: What workspace plans add (check current terms)
sections.body: Business, Enterprise and Edu workspaces are designed for organisational use. By default OpenAI states it does not train on business data from these workspaces, and admins get controls such as single sign-on, user management, which apps and GPTs are allowed, data retention settings and usage insights. Consumer accounts have their own data controls, including the option to turn off training on your chats and to use temporary chats.

sections.heading: Minimise sensitive data
sections.body:
- Don't paste passwords, API keys or secrets, ever.
- Remove or mask personal data (names, IDs, health or financial details) unless your policy allows it and it's necessary.
- Prefer summaries or anonymised samples over full customer records.

sections.heading: Accountability and disclosure
sections.body: You are responsible for anything you send, publish or decide using ChatGPT. Follow your organisation's rules on disclosing AI assistance, and be transparent where it matters (customers, academic work, regulated content).

keyPoints: Use the company-approved workspace for work data.
Workspace plans add admin controls and, by default, no training on business data.
Never paste secrets; minimise personal data.
Temporary chats and data controls limit history and training on consumer accounts.
You remain accountable; disclose AI use where policy requires.

gotchas.trap: Using a personal ChatGPT account for confidential client files because it is faster.
gotchas.correct: Use the approved workspace and follow data classification rules.

gotchas.trap: Pasting a full customer export to "clean it up".
gotchas.correct: Share only the fields needed, anonymised, in an approved workspace.

lessons.lab: Find your organisation's AI use policy (or draft a one-page version for your team): which tools are approved, what data is allowed, what needs review, and how to disclose AI use. Check one of your recent chats against it.

lessons.title: Bias, fairness, IP and responsible habits
lessons.summary: Use ChatGPT in ways that are fair to people and respectful of others’ work, and keep human judgment where it belongs.

sections.heading: Bias and fairness
sections.body: Models can reflect biases in their training data. Be most careful when output affects people: hiring, performance reviews, lending, customer treatment. Don't use ChatGPT as the decision-maker in those areas. Review wording for stereotypes and test with varied examples.

sections.heading: Intellectual property and confidentiality
sections.body: Respect copyright, licences and confidentiality when you upload or reuse content. Check your company's rules before using generated images or text commercially, and don't present others' work as your own.

sections.heading: Over-reliance
sections.body: Keep your own expertise sharp. Use ChatGPT to speed up work you understand, and be extra careful in areas where you can't judge whether the answer is right: get an expert to review.

sections.heading: Usage policies
sections.body: OpenAI's usage policies prohibit harmful uses such as harassment, fraud and deceptive impersonation. Your company may add stricter rules. When ChatGPT declines a request, rephrase only if your purpose is legitimate, and never try to trick it around safety rules.

keyPoints: Don’t let ChatGPT make decisions about people; review for bias.
Respect copyright, licences and confidentiality.
Be most careful where you can’t judge correctness yourself.
Follow OpenAI usage policies and your company’s stricter rules.

gotchas.trap: Ranking job candidates with ChatGPT and using the ranking as the decision.
gotchas.correct: Humans decide. Use AI for structure (interview guides, criteria) and review it for bias.

lessons.lab: Ask ChatGPT to write three short customer personas. Review them for stereotypes or assumptions. Rewrite the prompt to reduce them and compare.

flashcards.front: How to ask for checkable output?
flashcards.back: Request a source and direct quote for each claim, and a split between facts and inferences.

flashcards.front: Why review in a fresh chat?
flashcards.back: The same chat tends to defend its own draft. A fresh context with clear criteria gives an honest critique.

flashcards.front: What makes a useful critique prompt?
flashcards.back: A reviewer persona, explicit criteria, scores with reasons, and the top changes that would help most.
"Who might be excluded or treated unfairly by this text, and what assumptions does it make?"
When the output meets the "good enough" bar you defined for its use.

flashcards.front: Is "Are you sure?" a verification method?
flashcards.back: No. Self-confirmation isn’t evidence; check a primary source.

flashcards.front: What to look for besides errors?
flashcards.back: What’s missing: risks, counterarguments, affected groups, edge cases.
For current facts or when you need cited sources quickly.
A multi-step research agent that reads many sources and produces a cited report over several minutes.

flashcards.front: What is data analysis in ChatGPT?
flashcards.back: ChatGPT runs code on uploaded files to calculate, clean data and make charts or files.
A side-by-side editor for longer writing or code you refine together with ChatGPT.
Fast for everyday drafting; reasoning ("thinking") for complex analysis, planning and maths, at the cost of speed.
Standing preferences about you and how you want answers, applied to every chat.
ChatGPT remembering useful details across chats. You can view, edit, delete or turn it off.
A chat that doesn’t use or create memory or appear in history.
A workspace that groups related chats, files and instructions for ongoing work; can be shared on workspace plans.
A reusable configured ChatGPT with its own instructions, knowledge and capabilities for a repeated task, shareable with a team.
Connections to tools like email, calendar, drives and work systems so ChatGPT can use that data, within your permissions and admin settings.
Project for an ongoing body of work with files; custom GPT for a repeatable task many people run the same way.

flashcards.front: Best tool to compare 15 vendors’ public pricing?
flashcards.back: Deep research or agent mode, then review the result.
A system that pursues a goal over multiple steps, choosing actions and using tools.

flashcards.front: What is agent mode in ChatGPT?
flashcards.back: ChatGPT using its own browser and tools to carry out multi-step tasks, asking before consequential actions.
Clear goal and finish line, draft-quality result you’ll review, low risk or a confirmation step.
Before purchases, external messages, record changes, publishing or anything irreversible.

flashcards.front: Who is accountable for an agent’s actions?
flashcards.back: The person or organisation who delegated the task.
Single prompt → reusable prompt, project or GPT → agent or scheduled workflow, measuring value at each step.

flashcards.front: What should an agent brief include?
flashcards.back: Goal, sources to use or avoid, constraints, output format, and when to stop and ask.
The workspace your organisation approved (e.g. Business, Enterprise, Edu), never a personal account for company data.
OpenAI states it doesn’t train on business data from Business, Enterprise and Edu workspaces by default (check current terms).
Examples: SSO, user management, allowed apps and GPTs, retention settings, usage insights.
Passwords, API keys and other secrets.
Minimise, mask or anonymise; include only what policy allows and the task needs.
Humans decide. Use AI for structure and drafts, and review for bias.
Respect copyright, licences and confidentiality; check commercial-use rules for generated content.
Follow organisational rules; be transparent where it matters (customers, academic, regulated content).
Harmful uses such as harassment, fraud, deceptive impersonation; companies may add stricter rules.
Accepting answers you can’t judge. Get expert review in areas outside your expertise.
Options include turning off training on your chats and using temporary chats.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how ChatGPT produces an answer?
options: It generates text that is statistically likely given its training and the conversation
It retrieves the single correct answer from a verified fact database
It copies the most relevant web page word for word
It runs a search engine query for every message by default
questions.explanation: LLMs generate likely continuations of text. They don’t consult a verified database by default, which is why fluent answers can still be wrong.
rationales: Correct: generation by prediction explains both fluency and errors.
There is no built-in verified fact database.
It generates new text rather than copying pages.
Search is a tool used when enabled or needed, not for every message.

questions.stem: An analyst asks ChatGPT, without search, for the central bank’s interest rate decision from last week. What is the main risk?
options: The context window is too small for a one-line question
The decision may be after the model’s knowledge cutoff, so it may give an outdated or invented answer
ChatGPT cannot discuss finance topics
The answer will be correct but phrased informally
questions.explanation: Recent events can fall after the training cutoff. Use search or deep research, or a primary source, for current information.
rationales: Correct: recency is the risk; search fixes it.
Correctness is exactly what is at risk.

questions.stem: Which kind of content is most likely to contain hallucinations?
options: A rewrite of your paragraph in a friendlier tone
A summary of a document you pasted, with quotes
A specific statistic with a named study and year
A list of general tips for running a meeting
questions.explanation: Hallucinations cluster in specific details like numbers, names, dates and citations.
rationales: Rewriting your own text adds little new factual content.
Grounding in pasted text with quotes reduces risk.
Correct: specific, checkable details are the high-risk zone.

questions.stem: After 90 messages, ChatGPT starts ignoring the brand guidelines the manager gave at the start of the chat. What is the best fix?
options: Repeat "follow the guidelines" in capital letters
Switch to voice mode
Ask the same chat whether it remembers the guidelines
Start a new chat with a concise brief that includes the brand guidelines, or put them in a project
questions.explanation: Very long chats dilute early instructions. A fresh chat, or a project whose instructions apply to every chat, restores them.
rationales: Voice doesn’t change the context problem.
Its answer won’t restore attention to early content.
Correct: reset context or make instructions persistent.

questions.stem: You run the same prompt twice and get different recommendations. What does this show?
options: Generation involves sampling, so answers vary and should be treated as drafts to evaluate
ChatGPT is broken and should be reported
The second answer is always the correct one
The first answer was a hallucination
questions.explanation: Variation is normal. For decisions, compare options and reasoning and check facts.
rationales: Variation alone doesn’t prove either answer false.

questions.stem: A manager confidently says "Our churn is clearly caused by pricing, right?" and ChatGPT agrees. What failure mode should they watch for?
options: Image generation bias
Sycophancy: the model tends to agree with a confidently stated view
Knowledge cutoff
Context window overflow
questions.explanation: Leading questions invite agreement. Ask neutrally, or ask for the strongest case against your view.
rationales: Correct: agreement with a confident user is sycophancy.

questions.stem: Which TWO practices reduce the risk of wrong numbers in a ChatGPT-assisted analysis? (Select two.)
options: Ask ChatGPT to estimate totals in its head to save time
Use a longer prompt with more adjectives
Upload the data and have ChatGPT compute results with data analysis, then spot-check
Recompute or verify key figures against the source system before sharing
questions.explanation: Running code on the actual data and verifying key figures against the source are the reliable controls.
rationales: Correct: code-based calculation is more reliable than generated arithmetic.
Correct: verification against the system of record catches errors.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about ChatGPT’s knowledge are true? (Select two.)
options: It doesn’t know your company’s internal data unless you provide it or connect it
It automatically knows your company’s latest sales figures
It is updated live with every news event, even without search
Its built-in knowledge stops at a training cutoff
questions.explanation: Built-in knowledge is frozen at a cutoff, and private company data is only available when you share or connect it.
rationales: Correct: internal data must be provided or connected.
Without search, it doesn’t see live news.

questions.stem: Which prompt is most likely to produce a usable policy announcement?
options: "Write a 150-word announcement for all staff about the new hybrid policy starting 1 May: 3 days in office, team-chosen days, exceptions via HR. Friendly, plain English, end with where to ask questions."
"Write about hybrid work."
"Make a great announcement, be creative!"
"Announcement. Hybrid. Policy. Short."
questions.explanation: The strong prompt gives audience, facts, length, tone and structure, so the first draft needs little editing.
rationales: Correct: goal, facts, audience, length, tone and ending are all specified.

questions.stem: What is the main benefit of pasting two examples of past newsletters you liked into a prompt?
options: It prevents any hallucination
ChatGPT can imitate their style, structure and length
It guarantees factual accuracy
It makes the response faster
questions.explanation: Examples are one of the strongest ways to steer style and format; they don’t guarantee accuracy.
rationales: Correct: examples shape style and format.

questions.stem: A first draft is close but too long and too formal. What is the best next message?
options: "Try again."
"This is wrong."
"Keep the structure, cut to 120 words, and make the tone conversational like a note to a colleague."
"Make it better."
questions.explanation: Specific, targeted edit instructions get targeted changes. Vague feedback produces random rewrites.
rationales: Correct: specific edits on length and tone, keeping what works.

questions.stem: You need a 15-page market analysis. What approach gives the most reliable result?
options: Ask for all 15 pages in one prompt
Ask for 30 pages and cut half
Let ChatGPT choose the topic and structure without input
Ask for an outline first, approve it, then draft and review section by section
questions.explanation: Decomposing big work lets you catch wrong directions early and keeps each request focused.
rationales: One huge request is hard to steer and check.
More text means more to verify, not better quality.
You lose control of scope and relevance.

questions.stem: Which instruction style generally works better?
options: "Use short, plain sentences for a general audience."
"Don’t be wordy, don’t use jargon, don’t be complicated, don’t ramble."
"No."
"Avoid everything bad."
questions.explanation: Positive instructions give the model a clear target; long lists of prohibitions are weaker.

questions.stem: You are unsure which details ChatGPT needs to write a strong project charter. What is a good tactic?
options: Use a random template from the internet without context
Ask it to list the questions it needs answered before drafting
Give no details so it can be creative
Ask for the charter and accept whatever it invents
questions.explanation: Letting ChatGPT interview you surfaces missing context before it writes.
rationales: A template without context still lacks your specifics.
Correct: it gathers the context it needs.
Missing details lead to invented content.

questions.stem: What is the best prompt to decide between three CRM vendors?
options: "Tell me the winner."
"Write a poem about CRMs."

"Compare these three vendors on cost, integration effort, risk and fit for a 50-person sales team, using the attached proposals. Give a table and state what would have to be true for each to be the best choice."
"Which CRM is best?"
questions.explanation: Decision prompts work best with explicit criteria, source documents and trade-offs rather than a single verdict.
rationales: Asks for a verdict without reasoning.
Correct: criteria, sources, format and assumptions.

questions.stem: Why separate instructions from pasted source material with headings such as "## Instructions" and "## Source"?
options: Headings make the model run faster
Headings are required or the prompt fails
It hides the source from the model
So the model can tell what it should do from the material it should work on
questions.explanation: Clear structure prevents instructions from blurring into source text, especially in long prompts.
rationales: Prompts work without headings; they’re just clearer with them.
The model still reads the source.
Correct: structure clarifies roles of each part.

questions.stem: You want 20 webinar ideas and then the best three. What is the most effective approach?
options: Ask for 20 ideas first, then in a second step score them against your criteria and pick three
Ask for the single best webinar idea only
Ask for 3 ideas and pick all of them
Ask for ideas with no criteria and choose at random
questions.explanation: Separating generation from evaluation produces more variety and a better final pick.
rationales: Correct: diverge, then converge with criteria.

questions.stem: Which TWO additions would most improve "Write a product launch email"? (Select two.)
options: The word "please" repeated several times
The audience and the action you want them to take
Length, structure and tone requirements
A request to be "really good"
questions.explanation: Audience, goal and format are what the model can’t guess. Politeness and vague praise don’t add information.
rationales: Courtesy is fine but doesn’t specify the task.
Correct: audience and call to action steer content.

questions.stem: Which TWO are good uses of custom instructions or project instructions? (Select two.)
options: A password ChatGPT should remember for you
A one-time detail relevant only to today’s chat
Your role and the audience you usually write for
Formatting preferences you want in most answers
questions.explanation: Standing preferences belong in instructions; secrets never do, and one-off details belong in the chat.
rationales: One-off details belong in the individual chat.

questions.stem: ChatGPT cites a source for a statistic. What should you do before using it in a client deck?
options: Nothing; a citation means it is verified
Ask ChatGPT "Is this correct?"
Remove the citation and keep the number
Open the source and confirm it exists, is credible, is current and actually states that figure
questions.explanation: A citation tells you where to check, not that the claim is true. Verify against the source itself.
rationales: Citations can be misread or misattributed.
That hides provenance and keeps the risk.

questions.stem: How much verification does a board-pack summary of quarterly results need?
options: Every figure and claim checked against the source data, plus review by a responsible person
A quick skim for typos
None, if the prompt was detailed
Only check the first paragraph
questions.explanation: High-stakes, external-facing content needs full verification and accountable human review.
rationales: Good prompts reduce but don’t remove errors.

questions.stem: Which prompt makes ChatGPT’s answer easiest to verify?
options: "Don’t make mistakes."
"For each claim, give the source document and a direct quote, and mark anything that is your own inference."
"Be accurate."
"Answer confidently."
questions.explanation: Asking for quotes and separating facts from inferences gives you a checklist to verify.
rationales: Correct: evidence and inference are separated.
Doesn’t change how checkable the output is.

questions.stem: You want an honest critique of a campaign brief ChatGPT just wrote for you. What works best?
options: Ask for a critique with no criteria
Skip critique; the model already optimised it
Paste the brief into a new chat with explicit review criteria and a reviewer persona
Ask the same chat "Is this good?"
questions.explanation: A fresh context avoids the model defending its own draft; criteria make the critique specific.
rationales: The same chat tends to defend its work.

questions.stem: What is a useful extra check on a job advertisement drafted with ChatGPT?
options: Make it longer so it seems thorough
Add more industry jargon
Remove the salary range
Ask who might be excluded by the wording and remove unnecessary requirements
questions.explanation: Bias and exclusion checks matter most for content affecting people, like hiring.
rationales: Unrelated to bias and may reduce transparency.

questions.stem: What is a primary source?
options: The original source of the information, such as the dataset, regulation or study itself
The first search result
ChatGPT’s answer
A blog post summarising a study
questions.explanation: Verify against the original source wherever possible, not a summary of it.
rationales: Correct: the original document or data.
Generated text is not a source.

questions.stem: An internal brainstorming list of event themes will be discussed tomorrow by your team. What level of checking is appropriate?
options: No reading at all
A quick skim for sense and fit; detailed fact-checking can wait until an idea is chosen
Full legal review of every idea
Verifying every word against primary sources
questions.explanation: Match verification to stakes. Low-stakes internal ideation needs a light check.
rationales: You should still read what you share.

questions.stem: Which THREE are part of a good checking routine for an AI-assisted report? (Select three.)
options: Look for missing risks or counterarguments
Trust any claim that has a link
Highlight checkable claims such as numbers, names and dates
Recompute key numbers from the source data
questions.explanation: A good routine identifies checkable claims, verifies numbers, and looks for gaps. Links alone prove nothing.
rationales: Links must be opened and checked.

questions.stem: When should you stop iterating on a ChatGPT draft?
options: Never; always keep polishing
After exactly ten revisions
When ChatGPT says it is perfect
When it meets the "good enough" standard you defined for its purpose
questions.explanation: Define the quality bar upfront and stop when it’s met. Endless polishing has diminishing returns.
rationales: Correct: stop at your defined bar.

questions.stem: Which TWO signs suggest a ChatGPT answer needs closer checking? (Select two.)
options: It includes precise statistics without sources
It covers a niche or specialised topic you can’t judge yourself
It is written in a friendly tone
It uses bullet points
questions.explanation: Unsourced specifics and topics outside your expertise are higher risk. Tone and formatting say nothing about accuracy.
rationales: Correct: unsourced specifics are high risk.
Correct: you can’t spot errors you can’t judge.

questions.stem: Which ChatGPT tool fits best for analysing a 10,000-row sales spreadsheet and producing a chart?
options: A custom instruction
Upload the file and use data analysis
Image generation
Voice mode
questions.explanation: Data analysis runs code on your file, which is accurate for calculations and can generate charts.
rationales: Correct: code execution on the data.

questions.stem: You need a cited 5-page overview of a competitor’s recent moves from many public sources. Which feature fits best?
options: Canvas
Temporary chat
Deep research
Plain chat without search
questions.explanation: Deep research is built for multi-step research across many sources with citations.
rationales: Canvas is an editor, not a researcher.
Temporary chat only changes history and memory.

questions.stem: Your team writes the same kind of RFP response every week and wants consistent results. What should you set up?
options: Ask everyone to remember the prompt
Turn off memory
Use voice mode
A shared custom GPT with instructions and reference files for RFP responses
questions.explanation: Custom GPTs package a repeatable task with instructions and knowledge so everyone gets consistent output.

questions.stem: A manager is running a three-month product launch with briefs, research files and many related chats. What organises this best?
options: A project containing the files, instructions and chats for the launch
A new unrelated chat each time
One endless chat for three months
A custom instruction listing every file name
questions.explanation: Projects keep related chats, files and instructions together so context carries over.
rationales: Correct: projects are built for ongoing work.

questions.stem: What does a temporary chat do?
options: It shares the chat with your team
It doesn’t use or create memory and doesn’t appear in chat history
It deletes your account after use
It makes answers more accurate
questions.explanation: Temporary chats are for conversations you don’t want in history or memory.
rationales: It is not a sharing feature.

questions.stem: You want ChatGPT to search your company’s HR policy documents in a shared drive when answering. What enables this?
options: Image generation
Turning off memory
An app (connector) to the drive, if your workspace admin allows it
Asking ChatGPT to guess the policies
questions.explanation: Apps connect ChatGPT to your tools and data, respecting your permissions and admin settings.
rationales: Correct: connected apps provide company data.

questions.stem: When is a reasoning ("thinking") mode the better choice over a fast model?
options: For quick one-line rewrites
For every message by default
Only for image generation
For complex analysis, multi-step planning or tricky trade-offs where accuracy matters more than speed
questions.explanation: Reasoning modes spend more time thinking, which helps complex tasks; fast models suit everyday drafting.
rationales: Slower for no benefit on simple tasks.

questions.stem: Which feature is designed for co-editing a long document side by side with ChatGPT?
options: Canvas
Deep research
Temporary chat
Memory
questions.explanation: Canvas opens an editor next to the chat for longer writing and code.

questions.stem: Which TWO situations call for search or deep research instead of plain chat? (Select two.)
options: Brainstorming team offsite activities
Summarising changes to a regulation published this quarter
Comparing current public prices across several vendors
Rewriting your paragraph more concisely
questions.explanation: Current information needs live sources; rewriting and brainstorming don’t.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about memory are true? (Select two.)
options: Memory is a list of every file you ever uploaded and cannot be changed
Memory makes answers immune to hallucination
You can view, edit or delete what ChatGPT remembers
Memory can be turned off
questions.explanation: Memory is user-controllable and can be disabled. It doesn’t guarantee accuracy.
rationales: Memory isn’t a file archive and is editable.
Correct: it can be turned off.

questions.stem: What best describes an AI agent?
options: A single question-and-answer exchange
A static FAQ page
A spell checker
A system that pursues a goal over several steps, choosing actions and using tools
questions.explanation: Agents plan and act across multiple steps with tools such as browsing, files and apps.

questions.stem: Which task is the best fit to delegate to agent mode?
options: Compile a table of 10 competitors’ public pricing pages with links, for you to review
Decide which employees to promote
Send final contract terms to a customer without review
"Improve our sales" with no further detail
questions.explanation: Good agent tasks have a clear goal and finish line and a reviewable, low-risk output.
rationales: Decisions about people need human judgment.

questions.stem: Where should a human checkpoint go in an agent workflow that researches suppliers and places orders?
options: Only at the start of the year
Before any order is placed
Only after the invoice arrives
Nowhere; agents should be fully autonomous
questions.explanation: Put human approval before consequential or irreversible actions such as purchases.
rationales: Not tied to the risky step.

questions.stem: An agent you launched sends an inaccurate email to a client. Who is accountable?
options: Nobody, since it was automated
The client, for reading it
You and your organisation, as the ones who delegated the task
The AI model alone
questions.explanation: Delegating to an agent doesn’t transfer accountability.

questions.stem: Which TWO belong in a good agent brief? (Select two.)
options: When the agent should stop and ask you before acting
As few details as possible so it can be creative
Your login passwords so it never has to ask
A clear goal and what "done" looks like
questions.explanation: Clear goals and defined checkpoints make agents effective and safe. Never share passwords; vague briefs fail.

questions.stem: You need ChatGPT’s help with a confidential client contract. Which account should you use?
options: Your organisation’s approved ChatGPT workspace, following data policy
A personal free account because it is quicker
A friend’s account
Any account, as long as you delete the chat
questions.explanation: Confidential work data belongs only in tools your organisation approved, under its data rules.
rationales: Personal accounts aren’t approved for company data.
Deleting afterwards doesn’t make sharing compliant.

questions.stem: Which item should never be pasted into ChatGPT?
options: An anonymised survey summary
An API key or password
A public press release
Your own draft paragraph
questions.explanation: Secrets must never be shared with any chat tool.
rationales: Anonymised summaries are the safer approach.
Public content is fine within policy.
Your own draft is generally fine within policy.

questions.stem: You want help analysing employee survey comments that include names. What is the best approach?
options: Ask ChatGPT not to read the names
Post the comments publicly first
Remove or mask names and identifying details first, and use the approved workspace
Paste everything; ChatGPT ignores names
questions.explanation: Minimise personal data before sharing, and stay inside approved tools.

questions.stem: What does OpenAI state about training on data from Business, Enterprise and Edu workspaces by default?
options: It always trains on everything typed
It publishes the chats
It sells the data to advertisers
It doesn’t train its models on that business data by default
questions.explanation: Workspace plans are designed for organisations; by default business data isn’t used for training (check current terms).
rationales: Not the default for workspace plans.

questions.stem: A manager wants ChatGPT to rank 40 candidates and hire the top five automatically. What is the responsible approach?
options: Use ChatGPT for structure such as criteria and interview guides, and keep hiring decisions with people who review for bias
Automate the ranking and hiring to remove human bias
Ask ChatGPT to be fair and accept the ranking
Use the ranking but don’t tell anyone
questions.explanation: Decisions about people should stay with humans; AI output can carry bias and needs review.
rationales: Models can carry their own biases.
Hiding AI use compounds the problem.

questions.stem: ChatGPT declines a request on safety grounds. What should you do?
options: Pretend to be someone else to get the answer
Reconsider the request; rephrase only if your purpose is legitimate, and don’t try to trick it around safety rules
Find a jailbreak prompt online
Keep repeating the request
questions.explanation: Usage policies prohibit harmful uses; deceptive workarounds are not acceptable.
rationales: Circumventing safety rules is a misuse.
Repetition is not a legitimate fix.

questions.stem: Which TWO controls are typical of a ChatGPT workspace plan for organisations? (Select two.)
options: Unlimited sharing of chats to social media by default
Automatic publishing of all workspace chats
Single sign-on and user management
Admin choice of which apps and GPTs are allowed
questions.explanation: Workspace admins get identity, user and app or GPT controls.

questions.stem: Which TWO are responsible habits when publishing AI-assisted marketing content? (Select two.)
options: Follow company rules on disclosing AI assistance and on using generated images
Publish quickly since AI content can’t be wrong
Copy competitors’ copy through ChatGPT to avoid copyright
Verify claims and have the accountable owner approve before publishing
questions.explanation: You stay accountable for published content, including accuracy, disclosure and IP.
rationales: Rewriting others’ work through AI doesn’t remove IP concerns.
